patterns.name: builder
patterns.title: Stepwise Builder
patterns.intent: Assemble a value a field at a time, so that a half-finished one cannot be mistaken for a finished one and the fields still owed are named where the mistake is made.

options.name: completeness
options.description: What happens when `build` is reached before every required field is set. `typestate` makes it a compile error naming the fields still owed, which is the version worth generating — the builder's type carries which fields have been supplied. `result` and `throw` check at run time instead, which is what a builder fed from a form or a config file needs, since the fields it will receive are not known statically.

options.name: collections
options.description: Emit `add`, which appends to a field whose value is an array and accepts only such a field. Off for a target with no collections, where the method would be unreachable surface.

options.name: includeTests
options.description: Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

patterns.provenance: Original implementation. "Builder" is from Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, "Design Patterns" (1994), where it separates the construction of a complex object from its representation. The book's version reports an unfinished object at run time or not at all; the typestate rendering here — a phantom type parameter accumulating the keys supplied, and a `build` member whose type names what is missing — is a TypeScript type-system construction adapted from no source.

patterns.name: factory
patterns.title: Typed Factory
patterns.intent: Construct one of several product types from a key, with the key narrowing the return type at compile time and untrusted keys handled at the boundary.

options.name: registration
options.description: Whether the set of kinds is closed. `static` fixes it at construction, which is the whole compile-time benefit. `dynamic` adds `extend`, returning a new factory whose type is widened by the creators added, so a plugin discovered at run time is still typed.

options.name: errorMode
options.description: How `from` reports a key it does not recognise. `result` returns a value carrying the unknown key and the ones it knows; `throw` raises an error carrying the same. Only `from` can fail — `create` takes a key the compiler has already checked.

options.name: context
options.description: Pass a shared context to every creator alongside the input, so creators can reach dependencies without closing over module state.

options.name: includeTests
options.description: Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

patterns.provenance: Original implementation. The factory idea is the Gang of Four's "Design Patterns" (1994), but nothing here is adapted from it: the book's formulation is a class hierarchy with a virtual constructor, and this is a key-indexed product map whose lookup narrows the return type, which is a TypeScript type-system construction with no equivalent in the original.

patterns.name: singleton
patterns.title: Singleton
patterns.intent: Guarantee that a type has one instance and give the program a way to reach it.
patterns.provenance: Advisory entry. "Singleton" is from Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, "Design Patterns" (1994), where a private constructor and a static accessor enforce single instantiation. No implementation is adapted, because none is offered: the guidance is the entry.

advisory.alternative: a module that exports the value
advisory.rationale: An ES module is already a singleton. The runtime evaluates it once per specifier and hands every later importer the same bindings, so single instantiation is a property of the module system rather than something a class has to defend. What the class adds on top is the part that hurts: a private constructor makes the value unconstructable in a test, so the suite that needs a second one for isolation has to reach past the accessor or reset shared state between cases, and the global reachability that made the pattern attractive is what makes those tests order-dependent. Exporting the value keeps the single instance and loses the ceremony; where a test genuinely needs its own, export the factory beside it and let the module hold the default.

patterns.name: prototype
patterns.title: Prototype
patterns.intent: Create an object by copying an existing one rather than by naming its class.
patterns.provenance: Advisory entry. "Prototype" is from Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, "Design Patterns" (1994), where a `clone` method on an abstract prototype produces new instances. No implementation is adapted; the guidance is the entry.

advisory.alternative: object spread for a shallow copy, or `structuredClone` for a deep one
advisory.rationale: The pattern exists because a language with nominal types and no object literals needs a virtual method to copy an object without naming its class. TypeScript needs neither: spread copies the fields a type declares and is checked against that type, and `structuredClone` — in every runtime this targets — deep-copies a value including Maps, Sets and Dates without the class having to cooperate. A hand-written `clone` in this setting is worse than the built-ins on the axis that matters, which is what happens when a field is added: spread and `structuredClone` carry it automatically, while `clone` keeps compiling and silently stops copying it.
advisory.example:
const draft = { ...template, title: "Second" }; // shallow, and typechecked
const deep = structuredClone(template); // nested Maps, Sets and Dates included
